narration: Right now, you can turn a tap and get clean water in seconds. In ancient Jerusalem, water could decide whether a whole city lived or died. Problem number one: the water was in the wrong place. The city's most reliable source, a spring in the valley, sat outside the walls. In a siege, an enemy could seize it, and the people inside would die of thirst. The Bible says King Hezekiah of Judah stopped the spring's upper outlet and brought its water down to the west side of the City of David. Most scholars connect this work with the threat of an Assyrian invasion, although the exact date is still debated. Problem number two: digging blind. Two teams started at opposite ends of a hill and cut toward each other through solid rock, in darkness, by lamplight. The finished tunnel runs about 533 meters, from the spring to a pool inside the city. And it is not straight. It curves like a snake. One idea is that the workers followed natural cracks in the rock, but historians still argue about it. Problem number three: proving it happened. In 1880, an inscription was found on the tunnel wall. It describes the final moments: the crews hearing each other's voices through the rock, then breaking through, pick against pick. Then the water flowed. So the next time you turn on a tap, remember the people who cut a river through a mountain, in the dark, to keep their city alive.
